clinicalPearls: Caused by usually de novo loss-of-function variants in CHD2, which encodes a chromatin remodelling enzyme that regulates gene expression during neurodevelopment rather than an ion channel
Presents as a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with onset typically in early childhood, often preceded by normal or near-normal early development
Myoclonic seizures are characteristic, and the phenotype frequently includes atonic, absence, and generalised tonic-clonic seizures with features overlapping myoclonic-atonic epilepsy
Photosensitivity and fixation-off sensitivity on electroencephalography are notable and relatively distinctive clues
Fever-triggered and prolonged seizures can occur, producing overlap with Dravet syndrome
Intellectual disability, autism spectrum features, and behavioural difficulties are common and may progress after seizure onset
Seizures are often drug-resistant, and broad-spectrum antiseizure agents are generally preferred over narrow sodium-channel-selective ones
reference.pathophysiology: CHD2 encodes chromodomain helicase DNA-binding protein 2, an ATP-dependent chromatin remodeller that repositions nucleosomes to regulate the transcription of genes important for neuronal development and function. Pathogenic variants, typically causing haploinsufficiency, disrupt the normal programme of gene expression during brain maturation. Unlike the direct membrane effects of channelopathies, the epileptogenic and neurodevelopmental consequences arise indirectly from dysregulated expression of downstream neuronal genes, destabilising network excitability and impairing cognitive and behavioural development. This transcriptional mechanism explains the mixed epilepsy and neurodevelopmental phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Other genetic generalised and photosensitive epilepsies
additionalInvestigations: Epilepsy gene panel or whole-exome sequencing to identify the CHD2 variant
Electroencephalography including photic stimulation to detect photosensitivity and fixation-off sensitivity
Brain magnetic resonance imaging to exclude structural causes
Seizure-trigger history including photosensitivity and fever
redFlags: Escalating myoclonic or atonic seizures with injury risk
reference.prognosis: Most affected individuals have drug-resistant epilepsy with intellectual disability and behavioural challenges, though seizure burden and cognitive outcome vary and some achieve partial seizure control.
pitfalls: Assuming an ion-channel mechanism and selecting narrow sodium-channel agents rather than broad-spectrum therapy
Missing photosensitivity and fixation-off sensitivity as diagnostic clues
Attributing the presentation solely to Dravet syndrome
Underestimating the autistic and behavioural comorbidity
references: ILAE resources on myoclonic and developmental and epileptic encephalopathies
management: Broad-spectrum antiseizure therapy targeting the myoclonic, atonic, absence and generalised tonic-clonic seizures, using agents such as valproate, levetiracetam, clobazam or benzodiazepines
Avoid sodium-channel-blocking antiseizure drugs that may aggravate myoclonic and generalised seizures
Reduce visual precipitants given photosensitivity and fixation-off sensitivity, with tinted lenses and screen precautions
Provide a rescue benzodiazepine plan for prolonged seizures and status epilepticus
Consider the ketogenic diet in drug-resistant epilepsy
Developmental, behavioural and educational support including therapies directed at autism-spectrum features and intellectual disability
Multidisciplinary care with epileptology and developmental paediatrics
Genetic counselling, noting the variant is usually de novo, with parental testing to inform recurrence risk
